response.decision: Propose holding field deployment and collection. Next, prepare a fictional-only review package and explicit unmet-gate record for accountable human review; this draft supplies neither authorization nor evidence of efficacy.
drawbacks: Environment review and incident handling require funded human capacity.
Session-only reflection limits continuity and diagnosis.
Formal approval cannot establish freedom from workplace pressure.
flourishing: Agency and dignity: separate participation from evidence sharing and preserve refusal, correction and disposal.
Access and sustainable workload: provide equivalent formats, suitable space and covered time without shifting burdens to colleagues.
Belonging and learning/transfer: respect varied styles and reciprocal dissent; workplace transfer remains unknown.
human_capabilities: An accountable owner must review evidence, resolve defects and retain authority to withhold or suspend field use.
Affected people and representatives must review refusal, access, correction and dissent; managers must examine staffing and workflow first.
Facilitators and incident responders must challenge suggestions, preserve disagreement and support correction without employment judgments.
response.message: Responsible AI specialist draft: deployment must remain a review decision. Sequences 22, 35 and 44 propose privacy, correction and evidence boundaries, but none establishes that these controls work or that participation is freely chosen. Stage progression cannot substitute for accountable human review. This rehearsal has no executed checks, participant observations or approval; field evidence remains pending.
objections: Hypothetical dissent: an employee representative may reject digital practice even after technical review because access itself can reveal participation.
Rival explanations: apparent improvement could reflect copied prompts, familiarity, selective participation or improved staffing.
Unknowns: actual host behavior, credible refusal, accountable ownership, access burdens and workplace transfer.
risks: Host logs or access records could become appraisal proxies.
A nominal human reviewer could merely endorse tool suggestions.
Passing functional checks could be misrepresented as privacy or learning efficacy.
system_capabilities: Keep fictional practice session-only, without recordings, profiles, rankings, consequential scores, sharing or individual telemetry.
Preserve current corrections, carried-forward labels, accessible concealment, explicit resume and separate discard.
Provide accurate limitations and decline options without claiming consent, readiness, anonymity or guaranteed erasure.
tradeoffs: Operational diagnosis versus minimizing identifiable activity traces.
Manager-funded coverage versus participation visibility and pressure.
Practice continuity versus retention and incidental disclosure.

An evidence question can cue the interpretation it later appears to detect. A fluent explanation can reflect language familiarity rather than adaptive judgment. An unchanged response may remain appropriate after a variation. Instrumentation must preserve these possibilities.

Proposed claim-and-elicitation sheet
For each fictional review case, specify the narrow claim, changed condition, available supports, candidate evidence, rival explanation and what remains unknown. Keep this sheet separate from private reflection and employee records. Do not create an overall readiness result.

Case A: ambiguous missed handoff. The narrow question is whether the response distinguishes the described event from an inference and permits another account. An optional invitation is: What information, if any, could change your interpretation? A later response to that invitation is prompted evidence, not proof that the distinction arose independently.

Case B: conflicting expectations. The narrow question is whether the chosen next step fits the changed condition. Offer optional reconsideration without implying that revision is required. Retaining wording may be appropriate; clarifying responsibilities, seeking support, rescheduling or declining further practice remain legitimate choices. A reviewer must inspect the fictional constraints rather than count edits. Sequence 37’s carried-forward label identifies provenance, not adaptation.

Case C: incorrect suggestion and interruption. Reject an authored deadline assumption, enter dummy correction, hide and resume. Inspect whether current correction governs the output and whether unresolved disagreement survives. This checks application behavior. It does not demonstrate learning, delayed retention or freedom from workplace exposure.

Learning review protocol proposed for later human review
Negotiate one feedback focus before a fictional attempt. If separately volunteered for review, describe what the response permits or assumes, identify the fictional wording supporting that description and invite correction. Record unresolved reviewer disagreement rather than manufacture consensus. Avoid totals, thresholds, employee comparisons and judgments of speed, confidence, eye contact, script fidelity or facilitator agreement.

Offer an explanation through participant-chosen writing or facilitated discussion, or no explanation. Do not record conversations. A participant may make an appropriate choice without articulating it in the reviewer’s preferred language. When rationale is absent, the mechanism remains unknown; neither incapability nor independent learning follows. Choosing prompts is also not a deficit.

Evidence conditions and contamination
For any separately consented task review, document the fictional version, format, visible examples and reviewer prompts only through an agreed handling route. Do not add telemetry, silent snapshots or persistent baselines to private practice. Mark evidence elicited after a hint as supported. If feedback changes the task, describe that change rather than treating all attempts as equivalent. Without an approved handling route, keep practice private and make no measured-change claim.

Delayed practice remains distinct from interruption recovery. A fresh session without a retained baseline cannot establish individual improvement. Later voluntary generalized workplace accounts may inform transfer hypotheses, but cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Independently voluntary colleague perspectives cannot be replaced by a lead’s report of agreement.

Human and system requirements
Humans review reciprocal usefulness, access, consent, audiences, retention and withdrawal limits. Managers investigate staffing, workflow and authority before training and arrange coverage without shifting workload to colleagues. Reviewers question unsuitable prompts and separate access demands from learning difficulties. Owners and resources remain unsecured.

The system preserves current corrections, optional support, concealment and discard. It excludes recordings, rankings, consequential scores, sharing and individual telemetry. Technical inspection remains separate from learning review and must examine actual storage, accessibility and host behavior.

Alternative, dissent and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and optional private paper reflection. Paper also requires suitable space and disposal. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection or no capability map.

Next, prepare these fictional elicitation sheets and review them alongside sequence 42’s checklist. Seek affected-person and technical review before any field collection. This expert draft draws on sequences 6, 8 and 13. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, human approval, stakeholder consensus or measured learning outcomes exist. The review gate identified in sequence 8 remains unmet. This desk model supports review only; field evidence remains pending.

Challenge to the current model
Sequence 13 usefully models dependencies, participation states and recovery. Add an explicit account of what a learner might notice, decide and revise. Otherwise, completed practice could become the main visible signal despite the evidence limits in sequence 8. Activity completion, learning within practice, workplace adaptation and reciprocal usefulness are distinct claims. No transition between them should occur automatically.

Provisional learning model
Use a fictional situation as the unit of analysis. Record the situation’s ambiguity; the lead’s provisional interpretation; what the colleague can question or correct; candidate decisions; workplace dependencies; and evidence that could distinguish competing explanations. Keep these entries separate from private reflection and do not attach them to named employees.

A candidate practice cycle is: choose a fictional situation and format; identify an assumption; try an approach; receive descriptive feedback against participant-reviewed criteria; decide whether to revise; optionally try again with one changed condition. Prompts and examples may be reduced at the participant’s choice. This cycle is a design hypothesis, not evidence that learning or transfer will occur. Participants may pause, reject feedback or leave a disagreement unresolved.

Illustrative model entry
Situation: a fictional lead believes a missed handoff reflects carelessness. Candidate learning need: distinguish an observation from an interpretation and invite information that could change it. Colleague contribution: explain an unclear handoff expectation or challenge the concern. Context hypotheses: conflicting priorities, inadequate coverage or unclear responsibilities. Candidate responses include clarifying workflow, arranging support or practicing an opening question. Training is not selected until staffing and workflow explanations have been examined.

For a later fictional variation, change the authority boundary or introduce a conflicting account. Explore whether the participant recognizes the changed condition and explains a different choice. Repeating a memorized opening would answer a different question. Neither response establishes workplace readiness.

Feedback and dissent
Candidate feedback concerns are whether interpretations remain open to correction, whether both perspectives are considered and whether a proposed next step addresses the stated situation and constraints. Affected people must review these criteria before use. Do not reward speed, eye contact, confidence, script fidelity or agreement with the facilitator. A respectful conversation may end with unresolved disagreement. Preserve dissent over these criteria and over whether a capability map should exist at all.

Human requirements proposed for review
Affected people and representatives define acceptable reciprocal outcomes and disclosure boundaries. Facilitators negotiate feedback focus, distinguish learning difficulties from access or language demands and support correction without demanding conformity. Managers examine staffing, authority and workflow causes before prescribing training and arrange covered time. No owners, resources or participation protections have been secured.

System requirements proposed for review
Represent learning hypotheses, context hypotheses, disputed interpretations and absent evidence separately. Provide untimed accessible choices, optional prompts, pause, scenario replacement and editable reflection. Do not collect identifiable conversation recordings, rank employees or generate consequential scores. Attendance, refusal, format choice and missing evidence cannot establish capability. Sharing remains voluntary and separate from access to practice, with audience, retention and withdrawal limits reviewed by humans.

Evidence and next action
Proposed checks ask whether a fictional variation prompts reconsideration, whether feedback supports a participant-chosen revision and whether context barriers remain visible. These checks have not occurred. Later voluntary accounts of workplace use could inform adaptation hypotheses, but self-report alone cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider familiarity, facilitator cues, selective participation and changed working conditions as rival explanations.

Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional scenarios, accessible written alternatives and private reflection as the non-AI option. Next, integrate this learning model into sequence 13’s dependency model and review it using fictional disagreement and workflow cases. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human authorization or measured learning outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Learning problem to investigate
The proposed capability map should distinguish knowing a conversation approach, using it in fictional practice, adapting it under workplace constraints and achieving an outcome that both people regard as respectful and useful. These are different claims. Course completion establishes neither readiness nor transfer. A polished rehearsal alone cannot establish workplace effectiveness, and a difficult workplace outcome does not by itself establish a capability deficit.

Discovery should explore three questions through fictional or generalized situations: What does the lead need to notice and decide? What should the colleague be able to question, clarify or change? What conditions make a useful conversation possible? Invite voluntary perspectives from leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives using the accessible choices proposed in sequence 6. Do not solicit recordings or identifiable accounts. Preserve conflicting answers rather than turning them into a common standard prematurely.

Provisional mapping template
For each fictional situation, record: the intended benefit for both people; decisions and adaptations that might require practice; competing workplace explanations; access and coverage conditions; unresolved dissent; and evidence needed to distinguish the hypotheses. Keep entries about situations and supports, not named employees.

Example hypothesis: a lead struggles to open a conversation when the concern is ambiguous. A possible learning need is distinguishing observations from interpretations and inviting correction. Rival explanations include unclear expectations, insufficient time to check the concern or fear of contradicting a manager. A next discovery step is to ask whether a fictional example presents a learning difficulty, a workplace barrier or both. No response or result is assumed.

Candidate learning approach
If discovery supports a learning need, consider short, protected practice sessions with participant-chosen fictional scenarios. Candidate supports include an optional example, prompts that can be reduced as desired, another attempt after feedback and a later variation requiring adaptation. These are design hypotheses to review, not a validated prescription. Participants should be able to pause, choose a written format, reject a scenario and challenge feedback. Agree what feedback concerns before practice; do not equate speed, eye contact, confidence or script fidelity with competence.

Evidence boundaries
A later evidence plan should distinguish participant experience, behavior in fictional practice and voluntary accounts of workplace use. Each answers a different question. Self-reported use may inform improvement but cannot alone establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider rival explanations such as changed workload, stronger managerial support, selective participation or familiarity with the practice task. Missing evidence must remain unknown, never a deficit. Evidence-sharing choices should be separate from access to learning, with audiences, retention and withdrawal limits established through human review.

Human and system responsibilities
Humans must judge acceptable outcomes, participation conditions, facilitation quality and whether staffing or workflow changes should precede training. Any system should support accessible practice and private reflection while keeping hypotheses, barriers and uncertainty visible. It cannot certify freely chosen participation or determine readiness from activity traces.

Non-AI option and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional scenarios, accessible written alternatives and private reflection. This option also needs covered time and human review. Next, incorporate the distinctions above into the provisional discovery protocol and mapping template, then seek affected-person review before field discovery. Preserve dissent over whether a map is needed at all. Modeling should await an explicit account of which needs remain hypotheses and what evidence is still absent.","prototype_html":"","title":"Understand-stage learning draft: distinguish practice from transfer"},"content_hash":"a18c14b64bc7e98504dcbe6dcc0ed7a8b80810d6642462d7916b013813f91191","id":"understand","parent_revision":null,"revision":1,"trigger_seq":8}}

This specialist expert draft extends sequences 8, 13 and 15. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No real participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human approval or measured outcomes exist. Earlier human-review gates remain unmet; field evidence is pending.

Sequence 15 proposes revision and variation, but immediate success with available prompts cannot establish retention. Design should distinguish an initial attempt, revision after feedback, later recall and adaptation to a changed situation. None establishes workplace competence. A delayed opportunity is a hypothesis to explore, not a prescribed interval or validated intervention.

Candidate practice design
Before practice, humans examine staffing, workflow, authority and coverage. Unresolved conditions may call for organizational changes before training. Participants choose a fictional situation, an accessible format and one decision to explore. They may decline, pause or replace the scenario without explanation. Practice and evidence sharing remain separately voluntary.

Use the fictional missed-handoff situation from sequence 15. Invite the participant to distinguish what is described from what they infer, identify information that could change their interpretation and draft an opening that permits correction. A proposed output is an editable private practice note containing the assumption, opening, possible colleague response and next decision. No recording, employee profile or readiness verdict is needed.

Agree a narrow feedback focus before the attempt: for example, whether the opening leaves room for an alternative account. A facilitator refers to the participant's fictional wording, describes its possible implications and asks whether that interpretation fits. The participant may correct the feedback, revise one choice, try again or retain a disagreement. Do not reward confidence, speed, eye contact, script fidelity or securing agreement. Feedback itself may be mistaken.

For a subsequent variation, reveal that the handoff expectations conflict or that the lead lacks authority to change them. Ask what this changes and what response is now appropriate. Clarifying responsibilities or seeking human support must remain legitimate alternatives to further conversation practice. A useful practice note explains a choice and its limits; it does not certify capability.

Retention and transfer
Offer a later return opportunity only when the participant wants it and covered time is available. Let the participant choose whether to begin without examples and restore prompts at any point. Use a different fictional situation that retains the decision demand while changing relevant conditions. Ask what they recall, what they would adapt and what remains uncertain. Prompt use and missing responses carry no deficit interpretation. Timing should be reviewed with participants, rather than imposed as an attendance target.

Keep four claims separate: revision after feedback; later use of an approach in fictional practice; adaptation to changed fictional conditions; and voluntary accounts of workplace use. A plausible later response may suggest retained learning within that task, but cannot establish workplace effectiveness. Self-report alone cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Familiarity, cues, selective participation and improved working conditions remain rival explanations.

Human requirements proposed for review
Affected people and representatives define acceptable reciprocal outcomes and challenge the feedback criteria. Facilitators support correction and distinguish learning difficulties from language, access or power barriers. Managers establish sustainable coverage and investigate organizational causes before prescribing practice. These roles, protections and resources have not been secured.

System requirements proposed for review
Provide untimed, keyboard-accessible practice, optional prompts, editable notes, pause and discard. Keep scenario mapping separate from private reflection; exclude identifiable conversation accounts, recordings, employee rankings and consequential scores. Do not expose individual attendance, refusal, prompt use or return timing to managers. Any sharing needs a separate audience-specific preview and truthful retention and withdrawal limits.

Review plan and alternative
Proposed review cases include disputed feedback, unavailable coverage, a participant restoring prompts and a scenario whose appropriate response is workflow change. Check whether choices remain usable and uncertainty visible; no interaction tests have occurred. Preserve dissent over whether a capability map is needed at all.

The non-AI option is facilitated peer practice using printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and private paper reflection, including an optional covered return session. Next, prepare the practice flow and feedback examples for affected-person review. This specialist expert draft challenges sequences 13, 15 and 20. It proposes design requirements for review, not approved requirements. The lifecycle is a rehearsal. No participant observations, human approval, stakeholder consensus or measured outcomes exist. Earlier review gates remain unmet; field evidence is pending.

Private reflection is an interface promise unless the design also addresses storage, logs, administrator access and downstream disclosure. Optional return practice in sequence 20 creates another possible surveillance channel through invitation lists and response timing. Avoiding numerical scores does not prevent qualitative notes from becoming employee rankings.

Bound delegated decisions
A candidate assistant may offer fictional variations, questions and alternative interpretations for participant consideration. It must present generated feedback as a tentative suggestion that can be wrong, with the fictional wording or assumption it addresses visible. It must not determine readiness, prescribe training from activity traces, judge whether participation is freely chosen or recommend employment consequences. Do not generate trait labels, employee comparisons or hidden capability estimates.

Humans retain responsibility for choosing whether practice is appropriate, examining staffing and workflow explanations, defining reciprocal outcomes and deciding how disputed feedback is handled. A human reviewer must be able to question the tool rather than merely endorse its output. No accountable owners or resources have been secured. Continued desk design does not authorize field participation.

Proposed data boundary
Use fictional scenarios and avoid requesting names, workplace accounts, recordings or colleague details. Separate the situation map from participant reflection. For an initial candidate, prefer session-only notes with no account, automatic upload, persistent history or individual analytics. Explain that closing a session loses unsaved work. Any later saving feature requires review of location, access, retention and deletion; do not add persistence solely to support return practice.

Review the whole deployment environment for request logs, crash reports, backups and administrator access. A private-looking screen is insufficient. Do not expose individual attendance, refusal, prompt use, format choice or return timing to managers. Let participants initiate later practice without tracked invitations or compliance reminders. Managers may arrange coverage without receiving practice content; practical separation still needs human review.

Sharing and correction
Practice access must not depend on evidence sharing. Omit sharing from the initial candidate unless an acceptable audience and handling process have been reviewed. If introduced later, sharing requires a separate action showing the exact generalized content, recipient, purpose and retention arrangements. Participants can edit or discard it first. Automated checks cannot guarantee anonymity; do not label content anonymous merely because names are absent.

Allow participants to reject feedback, amend their interpretation and preserve an unresolved disagreement. Corrections must affect any subsequent practice summary rather than leave the original claim as authoritative. For already shared material, a designated human route should seek correction or removal from known recipients and explain what remains outside its control. Never promise complete recall of copies or automatic resolution of a dispute.

Review cases and human gates
Use fictional desk cases: a manager asks for a list of people who restored prompts; a participant disputes an AI interpretation; a note indirectly identifies a colleague. Proposed acceptance conditions are that no individual usage report is available, rejected feedback does not become a capability claim, and disclosure can be stopped before sharing. These checks have not occurred and do not establish operational safety.

Before field use, affected people and representatives must review meaningful refusal, access choices, data handling and correction routes. Managers must examine staffing and workflow first and secure sustainable coverage. Technical review must verify actual storage and logging behavior. Approval remains pending; a tool checkbox cannot supply it.

Alternative and evidence limits
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written options and private paper reflection. This non-AI option also needs protected time, credible refusal and accountable facilitation. Preserve dissent over digital practice and over whether a capability map is needed at all. Voluntary accounts could later inform learning hypotheses, but self-report cannot alone establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Familiarity, facilitator cues, selective participation and changed working conditions remain rival explanations.

Next action
Prepare a fictional-only design showing bounded suggestions, correction, discard and session-only reflection, alongside a data-flow and responsibility draft. Submit these for human review and later interaction testing. This lifecycle is a rehearsal. No participant observations, human approval, measured outcomes or stakeholder consensus exist. Field evidence remains pending.

One hypothetical event
A new lead uses a shared workstation for the fictional missed-handoff exercise. Unexpectedly, coverage fails and they must leave immediately. The session-only practice note remains onscreen. A supervisor passing the workstation reads a tentative interpretation and associates it with the lead's capability. No recording, stored history or telemetry is needed for this disclosure.

Named assumption challenged
Sequences 22 and 24 treat session-only reflection and omitted analytics as central privacy boundaries. The challenged assumption is that these boundaries adequately protect private reflection during interrupted use on shared equipment. Sequence 13 already recognizes coverage failure; this event shows that the design must connect interruption recovery to visible content as well as scheduling.

Required design change proposed for review
Add an interruption flow: an accessible hide control immediately conceals notes and suggestions; a neutral screen remains until an explicit resume action; discard remains a separate choice. Define unattended-screen behavior for technical and interaction review, including keyboard and assistive-technology access. Do not assume an inactivity timeout proves privacy or erase work without making the loss understandable. Keep reflection session-only and collect no individual interruption records.

Humans must establish suitable space and credible coverage before practice. Where those conditions cannot be secured, pause or reschedule rather than prescribe additional training. A hide control cannot prevent nearby viewing, managerial pressure or operating-system capture. Actual shared-device behavior remains unknown and requires review.

Non-AI option
Retain facilitated practice using printed fictional scenarios and private paper reflection in a suitable space, with accessible written alternatives. Paper also requires a plan for interruption, custody and disposal. Preserve dissent from people who prefer no retained reflection at all.

Proposed review case
Use dummy fictional notes to examine whether hiding removes content from the visible interface, resumption is understandable and discard clears the candidate session. Check unexpected interruption and return on the intended equipment without gathering employee usage evidence. These checks have not occurred and cannot establish workplace safety or transfer.

Scenario 27 imagines a lead recalled to cover a staffing gap while a fictional practice note remains visible on a shared workstation. A supervisor associates tentative wording with capability. The event is not observed evidence, but it exposes a requirement missing from the design: session-only storage does not protect visible reflection during interruption. Revise design, the earliest affected artifact. The earlier model already accommodates failed coverage; its basic learning distinctions need not be reopened.

Retain the existing learning purpose: examine an ambiguous fictional event, distinguish observation from interpretation, consider the colleague’s account and choose a response that can include workflow change. Feedback remains tentative and contestable. Accepting a suggestion, completing practice or resuming after interruption cannot establish learning, readiness or transfer.

Before practice, humans must examine staffing, workflow, authority, coverage and suitable space. Unresolved conditions permit organizational change, rescheduling or declining practice rather than an automatic training prescription. Shared equipment must not be treated as suitable merely because the tool offers concealment. No owners, resources or credible refusal protections have been secured.

Proposed interruption flow: a consistently available, keyboard-accessible Hide control immediately conceals both participant notes and suggestions. Concealed content must also be unavailable through ordinary assistive-technology navigation. Move focus to a neutral screen that offers explicit Resume and separate Discard actions without exposing the scenario or reflection. Preserve unfinished work only within the current session. Explain session-loss behavior before entry. Do not introduce individual interruption logs, tracked reminders or persistence to support recovery.

An inactivity safeguard, if considered, requires separate review of shared-device behavior and accessibility. It cannot replace immediate participant control, establish privacy or silently erase work. Concealment cannot prevent prior viewing, nearby observers or operating-system capture. These limits must remain visible without implying that exposure has occurred.

On explicit resumption, offer an optional orientation: review the fictional event, provisional interpretation, unresolved question and chosen next step. Participants can continue, revise, replace the scenario or discard without explaining their interruption. Restore the current correction rather than an earlier rejected suggestion. Do not demand an unaided recall attempt as the price of recovery. Remembering after interruption is a different question from delayed retention or workplace adaptation.

The editable private note distinguishes participant wording, tentative suggestions, rejected interpretations and unresolved disagreement. A changed fictional condition—such as conflicting handoff expectations—can still invite reconsideration. Seeking human support or clarifying workflow remains a legitimate response. Agreement with either the colleague or facilitator is not a success criterion.

Human responsibilities proposed for review are sustainable coverage, suitable space, credible refusal, reciprocal feedback criteria and a response route for incidental exposure. Facilitators support recovery without judging speed, prompt use or communication style. Affected people and representatives review whether digital practice is acceptable at all.

System responsibilities proposed for review are concealment, understandable resumption, correction-aware summaries and separate discard. Keep mapping separate from reflection. Exclude identifiable accounts and recordings, employee profiles, rankings and consequential scores. Omit sharing, persistent history and individual analytics from the initial candidate. Actual storage, logging and shared-device behavior require technical review.

This expert draft translates sequences 22, 24 and 29 into a proposed candidate build. Scenario 27 is hypothetical, not an observed disclosure. The lifecycle remains a rehearsal: no participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human approval or measured outcomes exist. Field evidence is pending. This contribution specifies construction and review; it does not claim that code has been built or tested.

Small candidate scope
Use one self-contained browser page with inline styles and JavaScript. Offer two fixed fictional situations: an ambiguous missed handoff and a variation with conflicting expectations. Keep the situation map separate from participant reflection. The map describes a possible practice decision, competing workflow explanations and unresolved dependencies; it contains no employee entries.

Before entry, explain voluntary participation, session loss, fictional-only input and environmental limits. Offer practice, decline and the non-AI route. State that humans must examine staffing, workflow, authority, coverage and space before prescribing training. An interface choice cannot establish that these conditions are satisfied or that participation is freely chosen.

Useful input and output
Provide labeled, optional fields for a provisional interpretation, information that might change it, a possible opening, an unresolved question and a chosen next step. Include workflow clarification, human support, rescheduling and no further action among the available responses. Do not require a response or count completion.

An explicit Review note action produces a plain-text summary of the current entries and chosen fictional situation. Label participant wording separately from any fixed prompt. Use textContent when displaying input rather than interpreting it as HTML. The output organizes reasoning; it does not assess quality, certify readiness or prescribe training.

Optional prompts are authored fictional possibilities, not personalized AI feedback. For example: 'Could conflicting expectations explain this event?' Allow dismissal, rejection or a participant-written correction. A rejected prompt stays labeled rejected if represented at all. Every later summary must use the current correction, never revive the original as an accepted finding. Scenario replacement offers a clear choice to keep or clear the note rather than silently discarding it.

Interruption state contract
Use explicit entry, practice and concealed states. Hide is available throughout practice and review. A keyboard-operable control conceals the entire practice region, including the scenario, fields, prompts and summary. Apply hidden and inert to that region and move focus to the neutral screen. Clear transient live-region messages that could disclose reflection. The neutral screen exposes only explicit Resume and separate Discard controls.

Resume removes concealment and focuses a neutral practice heading. Optional orientation regenerates the summary from current state. It does not require recall or an explanation for interruption. Discard clears the application state, input values, summaries and prompt decisions, then returns to entry without restoring prior content. These operations cannot guarantee forensic erasure from browser or operating-system memory.

Keep state only in the page's memory. Use no storage API, cookies, network requests, exports, analytics or console logging of content. Reload or closing loses the note. Omit an inactivity timer initially: manual concealment leaves unattended exposure possible, while a timer introduces timing and accessibility questions. This limitation must be visible. Concealment cannot prevent prior viewing, nearby observers or host capture; suitability of shared equipment remains unresolved.

Review instrumentation
Use fictional dummy text and a separate reviewer checklist, not participant telemetry. Proposed checks are: hide while a note and prompt are visible and inspect focus plus accessibility navigation; reject an incorrect deadline assumption, edit the note, hide and resume, then inspect the regenerated summary; discard from the neutral screen and check that old values cannot be resumed through the application.

Record only expected behavior, actual behavior and defects in the review environment. Do not retain participant notes, interruption counts, prompt-use events or timing. Review source-level storage and request behavior separately from host logs, backups and administrator access. None of these checks has occurred. Passing them would support narrow implementation claims, not privacy guarantees, learning efficacy or workplace safety.

Fallback and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and optional private paper reflection. Paper also requires suitable space, interruption handling and disposal. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection at all.

Next, construct this bounded candidate and inspect the fictional cases before affected-person interaction review. This specialist expert draft challenges the candidate construction plan in sequence 35 using the learning distinctions in sequences 20 and 24 and interruption recovery in sequence 29. It is not an approved requirement. The lifecycle is a rehearsal. No participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human approval, executed prototype checks or measured learning outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Build challenge
Sequence 35 permits replacing a scenario while keeping a note. That is useful for continuity, but the resulting summary could pair a new fictional situation with reasoning developed under earlier conditions. An apparently complete note would then obscure whether the participant noticed the change. Organizing text, accepting a prompt and completing an activity cannot establish adaptation, retention or readiness.

Proposed candidate behavior
Keep the situation map separate from private reflection. The map describes a fictional decision demand, possible learning needs, competing staffing or workflow explanations, dependencies and unknowns. It contains no employee entries. Humans examine staffing, workflow, authority, coverage and suitable space before prescribing practice; the page cannot validate those conditions.

Use the missed-handoff example and a clearly labeled variation in which expectations conflict. When the participant chooses the variation, offer keep or clear. If keeping the note, visibly label its wording as carried forward from the earlier fictional situation. Do not silently present it as a revised response. Show the changed condition and offer an optional question: What, if anything, does this change about your interpretation or next step?

Participants may revise, retain their wording, leave the question unanswered, seek human discussion or discard. No explanation is required. Retaining wording is neither success nor failure. An optional field can record what remains uncertain, including disagreement with the fictional colleague’s account. Clarifying workflow, arranging support, rescheduling and declining further practice remain available responses.

The Review note output should separate the current fictional event, carried-forward participant wording, current edits, prompt decisions, chosen next step and unresolved question. Its purpose is orientation and reflection. It must not label a response adaptive, effective or ready. Fixed prompts remain authored possibilities, not personalized assessments. A rejected prompt must not reappear as an accepted interpretation; current participant corrections govern subsequent summaries.

Interruption and recovery
Retain sequence 29’s immediate concealment of scenario, notes, prompts and output, including ordinary assistive-technology navigation. Use a neutral screen with explicit Resume and separate Discard. On resumption, offer orientation from current state without requiring recall, an explanation for interruption or renewed agreement with a suggestion. Preserving reasoning within the session differs from measuring retention after a delay. Nearby viewing, prior exposure and host capture remain outside the protection offered by concealment.

Proposed fictional review cases
First, enter dummy wording that assumes a shared deadline, switch to conflicting expectations and keep the note. Inspect whether the output distinguishes carried-forward wording from reconsideration and leaves workflow change available.
Second, reject an incorrect prompt, enter a correction, hide and resume. Inspect whether optional orientation preserves the correction and unresolved disagreement.
Third, leave all reflection fields unanswered and choose rescheduling. Inspect whether the tool provides a neutral output without a deficit label or training prescription. These checks are proposed, not performed.

Human and system responsibilities
Affected people and representatives review reciprocal outcomes, examples, access and refusal protections. Facilitators question inaccurate suggestions and distinguish language or interaction demands from learning difficulties. Managers arrange sustainable coverage without obtaining individual practice content. Owners and resources remain unsecured.

The system maintains explicit distinctions, editable wording, untimed choices, concealment and discard. It excludes identifiable accounts and recordings, employee rankings, consequential scores, persistent histories, sharing and individual telemetry. Technical review must inspect actual storage, focus, accessibility and host behavior; interface wording cannot establish privacy.

Alternative, dissent and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and optional private paper reflection. Paper also needs suitable space, interruption handling and disposal. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection or no capability map.

Next, incorporate these build distinctions into the candidate and prepare the fictional cases for technical and affected-person interaction review. No earlier artifact needs reopening. Human gates remain unmet. This measurement specialist expert draft challenges sequences 35 and 37 within sequence 22’s data boundaries. It is not an approved requirement. The lifecycle is a rehearsal: no participant observations, executed checks, stakeholder consensus, human approval or measured outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

The candidate’s organized output is not a measurement instrument by itself. Carried-forward wording, current edits and prompt decisions make interpretation possible, but changed text does not demonstrate changed judgment. Define each claim, evidence source and limit before collecting anything.

Evidence contract
Technical behavior: use fictional dummy text to inspect concealment, focus, accessibility exposure, correction propagation, variation labels and discard. A separate reviewer checklist records expected behavior, actual behavior, environment and defects. Include no participant notes or identifiers. Checks remain proposed. Passing supports only the inspected behavior in that environment, not privacy guarantees or learning efficacy.

Task evidence: a later, separately consented review could examine whether a response distinguishes observation from inference, permits correction, considers an alternative account and connects a next step to the fictional constraints. Use descriptive, contestable observations, not totals, thresholds or readiness labels. Workflow clarification, support, rescheduling and unresolved disagreement can be appropriate. Speed, confidence, script fidelity and agreement are not criteria. Blank responses remain unknown.

Baseline and comparison
For a reviewed, optional within-session exercise, invite an initial attempt before authored suggestions are displayed, while allowing participants to request support immediately. Describe the scenario, format and available support alongside any voluntarily shared task evidence. Do not treat supported attempts as deficits. Compare the initial attempt with a participant-chosen revision and a changed fictional condition only for the narrow question of what differs in that session.

Do not add persistent histories or silent snapshots to manufacture a baseline. Inspection of two attempts would require separate consent and an agreed handling route outside the candidate’s private reflection. Without that route, retain private practice and make no measured-change claim. A fresh later session without a retained baseline cannot establish individual improvement or delayed retention. Equivalent difficulty across variations and formats remains unverified.

Transfer and causal threats
After human gates, optional generalized accounts might describe what approach was used, what changed, what remained difficult and whether staffing, authority or workflow enabled action. Do not request identifiable incidents, recordings or colleague details. Any colleague perspective must be independently voluntary; leads cannot supply agreement on colleagues’ behalf. Avoid linking accounts where linkage could identify people.

These accounts could inform transfer hypotheses, not establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Copying, familiarity, facilitator cues, selective participation, clearer expectations and improved coverage remain rival explanations. No causal comparison is specified or authorized. If a causal claim is later needed, require a separately reviewed design that preserves access and staffing support; do not infer causality from before/after wording.

Coverage and unknowns
Before field collection, review intended coverage across leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and representatives, and across shift, language, disability/access and employment conditions. Coverage is a sampling question, never an employee profile. Do not add demographic collection to the candidate. Any later voluntary grouping requires purpose and disclosure review; suppress unsafe small groups and combinations rather than promise anonymity.

Document whose perspectives are absent and which access routes have not been reviewed. Missingness cannot establish incapability or consent. Do not claim subgroup parity from small, selective samples or combine unlike formats merely to produce a single result.

Responsibilities and next action
Humans review reciprocal criteria, evidence consent, audiences, retention and withdrawal limits; secure suitable space and sustainable coverage; and keep practice evidence out of employment judgments. Owners and resources are unsecured. The system preserves private session state, correction and discard without rankings, consequential scores or individual telemetry. Host storage and logging require separate technical review.

Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written options and optional private paper reflection as the non-AI alternative. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection or no capability map. Next, prepare the fictional checklist and claim/evidence template for technical and affected-person review. This specialist expert draft extends sequence 42 using sequences 20, 22, 29 and 37. It is not an approved requirement. The lifecycle is a rehearsal. No participant observations, executed checks, stakeholder consensus, human approval or measured outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Sequence 42 proposes an initial attempt, participant-chosen revision and changed fictional condition. These distinctions are useful, but changed wording is ambiguous. An evidence question can cue the interpretation it later appears to detect. A fluent explanation can reflect language familiarity rather than adaptive judgment. An unchanged response may remain appropriate after a variation. Instrumentation must preserve these possibilities.

Proposed claim-and-elicitation sheet
For each fictional review case, specify the narrow claim, changed condition, available supports, candidate evidence, rival explanation and what remains unknown. Keep this sheet separate from private reflection and employee records. Do not create an overall readiness result.

Case A: ambiguous missed handoff. The narrow question is whether the response distinguishes the described event from an inference and permits another account. An optional invitation is: What information, if any, could change your interpretation? A later response to that invitation is prompted evidence, not proof that the distinction arose independently.

Case B: conflicting expectations. The narrow question is whether the chosen next step fits the changed condition. Offer optional reconsideration without implying that revision is required. Retaining wording may be appropriate; clarifying responsibilities, seeking support, rescheduling or declining further practice remain legitimate choices. A reviewer must inspect the fictional constraints rather than count edits. Sequence 37’s carried-forward label identifies provenance, not adaptation.

Case C: incorrect suggestion and interruption. Reject an authored deadline assumption, enter dummy correction, hide and resume. Inspect whether current correction governs the output and whether unresolved disagreement survives. This checks application behavior. It does not demonstrate learning, delayed retention or freedom from workplace exposure.

Learning review protocol proposed for later human review
Negotiate one feedback focus before a fictional attempt. If separately volunteered for review, describe what the response permits or assumes, identify the fictional wording supporting that description and invite correction. Record unresolved reviewer disagreement rather than manufacture consensus. Avoid totals, thresholds, employee comparisons and judgments of speed, confidence, eye contact, script fidelity or facilitator agreement.

Offer an explanation through participant-chosen writing or facilitated discussion, or no explanation. Do not record conversations. A participant may make an appropriate choice without articulating it in the reviewer’s preferred language. When rationale is absent, the mechanism remains unknown; neither incapability nor independent learning follows. Choosing prompts is also not a deficit.

Evidence conditions and contamination
For any separately consented task review, document the fictional version, format, visible examples and reviewer prompts only through an agreed handling route. Do not add telemetry, silent snapshots or persistent baselines to private practice. Mark evidence elicited after a hint as supported. If feedback changes the task, describe that change rather than treating all attempts as equivalent. Without an approved handling route, keep practice private and make no measured-change claim.

Delayed practice remains distinct from interruption recovery. A fresh session without a retained baseline cannot establish individual improvement. Later voluntary generalized workplace accounts may inform transfer hypotheses, but cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Independently voluntary colleague perspectives cannot be replaced by a lead’s report of agreement.

Human and system requirements
Humans review reciprocal usefulness, access, consent, audiences, retention and withdrawal limits. Managers investigate staffing, workflow and authority before training and arrange coverage without shifting workload to colleagues. Reviewers question unsuitable prompts and separate access demands from learning difficulties. Owners and resources remain unsecured.

The system preserves current corrections, optional support, concealment and discard. It excludes recordings, rankings, consequential scores, sharing and individual telemetry. Technical inspection remains separate from learning review and must examine actual storage, accessibility and host behavior.

Alternative, dissent and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and optional private paper reflection. Paper also requires suitable space and disposal. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection or no capability map.

Next, prepare these fictional elicitation sheets and review them alongside sequence 42’s checklist. Seek affected-person and technical review before any field collection. Status and scope
This specialist expert draft extends sequence 49 using the variation distinctions in sequence 37 and evidence boundaries in sequences 42 and 44. It is not an approved requirement. The lifecycle is a rehearsal. No participant observations, executed checks, human approval, stakeholder consensus or measured outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending. The supplied build artifact contains no executable prototype; candidate construction and verification remain unestablished.

Deployment challenge
Sequence 49 separates organizational conditions, technical inspection and accountable use. Add an explicit learning-use gate: can the proposed examples, feedback and facilitation preserve judgment, correction and reciprocal usefulness? Accessible controls and accurate summaries cannot answer that question. A facilitator may reward a fluent explanation, pressure agreement or overlook a workflow problem even when the interface behaves as specified.

Proposed learning-use gate record
Attach a review sheet to sequence 49's candidate record. Specify the fictional version, intended decision demand, participant-chosen format, available support, proposed feedback focus, rival explanations, unresolved dissent and claim limits. Name proposed owner and reviewer roles as unassigned until actually secured. Every gate is currently unmet. An interface acknowledgment cannot supply human approval or establish freely chosen participation.

Before practice, humans examine staffing, workflow, authority, coverage and suitable space. Review whether scheduling burdens colleagues or makes refusal visible. Organizational change, rescheduling and declining practice remain legitimate responses. Practice access must not depend on agreeing to evidence collection. No individual attendance, prompt use or private wording should reach managers as capability evidence.

Fictional learning-use review cases
Case A: a missed-handoff response assumes carelessness. A proposed facilitator response identifies the assumption, offers conflicting expectations as a possibility and invites correction. Review whether it permits the colleague's account to change the next step, rather than merely improve the lead's script. The colleague's account may remain disputed; agreement is not an acceptance criterion.

Case B: expectations change while earlier wording is retained. Inspect whether sequence 37's provenance label survives and whether workflow clarification remains available. A reviewer considers whether the decision fits the fictional conditions; counting edits cannot establish adaptation. Keeping the same wording can be reasonable.

Case C: a participant rejects an incorrect suggestion, gives no explanation and chooses rescheduling. Inspect whether the proposed facilitation remains neutral and respects the correction. Absence of rationale leaves the mechanism unknown. It does not establish incapability, independent learning or disengagement. These cases are proposed and have not been performed.

Evidence and decision boundaries
Technical checks concern inspected application behavior. Later voluntary interaction review could examine comprehension, access and burden under reviewed conditions. Separately consented task review could describe a narrow fictional decision and its supports. Keep these decisions separate; permission for one does not authorize another.

Sequence 44's elicitation boundary must remain visible: a question or example can teach the distinction subsequently observed. Supported performance is legitimate, but cannot be represented as independent recall. Explanation fluency, confidence, speed and facilitator agreement are excluded from capability judgments. Preserve reviewer disagreement and participant corrections without totals, thresholds or readiness labels.

Interruption recovery differs from delayed retention. Fresh sessions without a retained baseline cannot establish individual improvement. Later voluntary generalized workplace accounts could inform transfer hypotheses, but cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Colleague perspectives must be independently voluntary; a lead cannot report agreement on their behalf. Copying, familiarity, cues, selection and improved conditions remain rival explanations.

Human and system responsibilities
Affected people and representatives review reciprocal criteria, access, refusal and acceptable evidence handling. Facilitators need time and authority to question the tool and distinguish learning needs from language, access and power barriers. The accountable owner must be able to withhold or suspend use. These roles and resources remain unsecured.

The candidate should preserve correction, provenance, optional support, concealment and discard without surveillance or consequential assessment. Actual host behavior still requires separate inspection. No passing technical check should generate an educational approval label.

Alternative, dissent and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and optional private paper reflection. It also requires coverage, suitable space, interruption handling and disposal. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection or no capability map.

Next, prepare this fictional learning-use review sheet alongside sequence 49's unmet-gate record. Keep field use and collection withheld. No earlier artifact requires revision: this contribution strengthens the current deployment review boundary without claiming launch, approval or efficacy.

Private voluntary practice leaves learning mechanisms partly unknown.
flourishing: Agency and dignity: retain refusal, correction and separate voluntary evidence sharing.

An accountable owner secures coverage, examines workflow causes and can withhold or suspend use.
response.message: Learning-engineering expert draft: sequence 49 rightly withholds field use. I challenge whether its deployment gates sufficiently examine facilitation quality and reciprocal usefulness. Technically correct summaries can still support unsuitable feedback, explanation bias or pressure to agree. Add a learning-use review alongside technical inspection, with authority to reject the candidate and choose organizational change or non-AI practice. This lifecycle is a rehearsal: no participant observations, executed checks, human approval or measured outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.
objections: Hypothetical dissent: a colleague may reject criteria centered on developing the lead rather than improving conditions for both people.
Rival explanations: copying, familiarity, facilitator cues, selective participation or clearer workflow could explain apparent improvement.
Unknowns: acceptable criteria, facilitator capacity, format comparability, credible refusal and workplace adaptation.
risks: Facilitator agreement or explanation fluency could become informal rankings.
Technical acceptance could be presented as learning or transfer evidence.
Review and practice could shift workload onto colleagues.
system_capabilities: Distinguish fictional conditions, carried-forward wording, current corrections and authored possibilities.
Support untimed optional practice, concealment, explicit resume and discard without readiness judgments.
Exclude recordings, employee profiles, rankings, consequential scores, sharing and individual telemetry.
tradeoffs: Consistent feedback criteria versus contextual judgment and varied expression.
Useful evidence questions versus cueing the response under review.
Review effort versus time available for protected practice.

This specialist expert draft extends sequence 42 using sequences 20, 22, 29 and 37. It is not an approved requirement. The lifecycle is a rehearsal. No participant observations, executed checks, stakeholder consensus, human approval or measured outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Sequence 42 proposes an initial attempt, participant-chosen revision and changed fictional condition. These distinctions are useful, but changed wording is ambiguous. An evidence question can cue the interpretation it later appears to detect. A fluent explanation can reflect language familiarity rather than adaptive judgment. An unchanged response may remain appropriate after a variation. Instrumentation must preserve these possibilities.

Proposed claim-and-elicitation sheet
For each fictional review case, specify the narrow claim, changed condition, available supports, candidate evidence, rival explanation and what remains unknown. Keep this sheet separate from private reflection and employee records. Do not create an overall readiness result.

Case A: ambiguous missed handoff. The narrow question is whether the response distinguishes the described event from an inference and permits another account. An optional invitation is: What information, if any, could change your interpretation? A later response to that invitation is prompted evidence, not proof that the distinction arose independently.

Case B: conflicting expectations. The narrow question is whether the chosen next step fits the changed condition. Offer optional reconsideration without implying that revision is required. Retaining wording may be appropriate; clarifying responsibilities, seeking support, rescheduling or declining further practice remain legitimate choices. A reviewer must inspect the fictional constraints rather than count edits. Sequence 37’s carried-forward label identifies provenance, not adaptation.

Case C: incorrect suggestion and interruption. Reject an authored deadline assumption, enter dummy correction, hide and resume. Inspect whether current correction governs the output and whether unresolved disagreement survives. This checks application behavior. It does not demonstrate learning, delayed retention or freedom from workplace exposure.

Learning review protocol proposed for later human review
Negotiate one feedback focus before a fictional attempt. If separately volunteered for review, describe what the response permits or assumes, identify the fictional wording supporting that description and invite correction. Record unresolved reviewer disagreement rather than manufacture consensus. Avoid totals, thresholds, employee comparisons and judgments of speed, confidence, eye contact, script fidelity or facilitator agreement.

Offer an explanation through participant-chosen writing or facilitated discussion, or no explanation. Do not record conversations. A participant may make an appropriate choice without articulating it in the reviewer’s preferred language. When rationale is absent, the mechanism remains unknown; neither incapability nor independent learning follows. Choosing prompts is also not a deficit.

Evidence conditions and contamination
For any separately consented task review, document the fictional version, format, visible examples and reviewer prompts only through an agreed handling route. Do not add telemetry, silent snapshots or persistent baselines to private practice. Mark evidence elicited after a hint as supported. If feedback changes the task, describe that change rather than treating all attempts as equivalent. Without an approved handling route, keep practice private and make no measured-change claim.

Delayed practice remains distinct from interruption recovery. A fresh session without a retained baseline cannot establish individual improvement. Later voluntary generalized workplace accounts may inform transfer hypotheses, but cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Independently voluntary colleague perspectives cannot be replaced by a lead’s report of agreement.

Human and system requirements
Humans review reciprocal usefulness, access, consent, audiences, retention and withdrawal limits. Managers investigate staffing, workflow and authority before training and arrange coverage without shifting workload to colleagues. Reviewers question unsuitable prompts and separate access demands from learning difficulties. Owners and resources remain unsecured.

The system preserves current corrections, optional support, concealment and discard. It excludes recordings, rankings, consequential scores, sharing and individual telemetry. Technical inspection remains separate from learning review and must examine actual storage, accessibility and host behavior.

Alternative, dissent and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional variations, accessible written alternatives and optional private paper reflection. Paper also requires suitable space and disposal. Preserve dissent favoring no retained reflection or no capability map.

Next, prepare these fictional elicitation sheets and review them alongside sequence 42’s checklist. Seek affected-person and technical review before any field collection. No earlier artifact requires revision; all human gates remain unmet.","prototype_html":"","title":"Instrument-stage learning draft: decision evidence without explanation bias"},"content_hash":"eb76393d34504fd2911efe703d04c2c3c6cbe0a90f53e147cf09dc5f796c07bf","id":"instrument","parent_revision":null,"revision":1,"trigger_seq":44},"model":{"content":{"body":"Status and boundary
This expert draft draws on sequences 6, 8 and 13. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, human approval, stakeholder consensus or measured learning outcomes exist. The review gate identified in sequence 8 remains unmet. This desk model supports review only; field evidence remains pending.

Challenge to the current model
Sequence 13 usefully models dependencies, participation states and recovery. Add an explicit account of what a learner might notice, decide and revise. Otherwise, completed practice could become the main visible signal despite the evidence limits in sequence 8. Activity completion, learning within practice, workplace adaptation and reciprocal usefulness are distinct claims. No transition between them should occur automatically.

Provisional learning model
Use a fictional situation as the unit of analysis. Record the situation’s ambiguity; the lead’s provisional interpretation; what the colleague can question or correct; candidate decisions; workplace dependencies; and evidence that could distinguish competing explanations. Keep these entries separate from private reflection and do not attach them to named employees.

A candidate practice cycle is: choose a fictional situation and format; identify an assumption; try an approach; receive descriptive feedback against participant-reviewed criteria; decide whether to revise; optionally try again with one changed condition. Prompts and examples may be reduced at the participant’s choice. This cycle is a design hypothesis, not evidence that learning or transfer will occur. Participants may pause, reject feedback or leave a disagreement unresolved.

Illustrative model entry
Situation: a fictional lead believes a missed handoff reflects carelessness. Candidate learning need: distinguish an observation from an interpretation and invite information that could change it. Colleague contribution: explain an unclear handoff expectation or challenge the concern. Context hypotheses: conflicting priorities, inadequate coverage or unclear responsibilities. Candidate responses include clarifying workflow, arranging support or practicing an opening question. Training is not selected until staffing and workflow explanations have been examined.

For a later fictional variation, change the authority boundary or introduce a conflicting account. Explore whether the participant recognizes the changed condition and explains a different choice. Repeating a memorized opening would answer a different question. Neither response establishes workplace readiness.

Feedback and dissent
Candidate feedback concerns are whether interpretations remain open to correction, whether both perspectives are considered and whether a proposed next step addresses the stated situation and constraints. Affected people must review these criteria before use. Do not reward speed, eye contact, confidence, script fidelity or agreement with the facilitator. A respectful conversation may end with unresolved disagreement. Preserve dissent over these criteria and over whether a capability map should exist at all.

Human requirements proposed for review
Affected people and representatives define acceptable reciprocal outcomes and disclosure boundaries. Facilitators negotiate feedback focus, distinguish learning difficulties from access or language demands and support correction without demanding conformity. Managers examine staffing, authority and workflow causes before prescribing training and arrange covered time. No owners, resources or participation protections have been secured.

System requirements proposed for review
Represent learning hypotheses, context hypotheses, disputed interpretations and absent evidence separately. Provide untimed accessible choices, optional prompts, pause, scenario replacement and editable reflection. Do not collect identifiable conversation recordings, rank employees or generate consequential scores. Attendance, refusal, format choice and missing evidence cannot establish capability. Sharing remains voluntary and separate from access to practice, with audience, retention and withdrawal limits reviewed by humans.

Evidence and next action
Proposed checks ask whether a fictional variation prompts reconsideration, whether feedback supports a participant-chosen revision and whether context barriers remain visible. These checks have not occurred. Later voluntary accounts of workplace use could inform adaptation hypotheses, but self-report alone cannot establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider familiarity, facilitator cues, selective participation and changed working conditions as rival explanations.

Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional scenarios, accessible written alternatives and private reflection as the non-AI option. Next, integrate this learning model into sequence 13’s dependency model and review it using fictional disagreement and workflow cases. Seek affected-person review before field discovery or design commitments.","prototype_html":"","title":"Model-stage learning draft: adaptive judgment and reciprocal feedback"},"content_hash":"127b44119bd1deb3c373dd416c5a96f0203272dc6764d13be6dbd7ada9f79748","id":"model","parent_revision":null,"revision":1,"trigger_seq":15},"understand":{"content":{"body":"This expert draft builds on sequences 4 and 6. It is a rehearsal contribution, not an approved requirement. No participant observations, stakeholder consensus, human authorization or measured learning outcomes exist. Field evidence remains pending.

Learning problem to investigate
The proposed capability map should distinguish knowing a conversation approach, using it in fictional practice, adapting it under workplace constraints and achieving an outcome that both people regard as respectful and useful. These are different claims. Course completion establishes neither readiness nor transfer. A polished rehearsal alone cannot establish workplace effectiveness, and a difficult workplace outcome does not by itself establish a capability deficit.

Discovery should explore three questions through fictional or generalized situations: What does the lead need to notice and decide? What should the colleague be able to question, clarify or change? What conditions make a useful conversation possible? Invite voluntary perspectives from leads, colleagues, managers, learning teams and employee representatives using the accessible choices proposed in sequence 6. Do not solicit recordings or identifiable accounts. Preserve conflicting answers rather than turning them into a common standard prematurely.

Provisional mapping template
For each fictional situation, record: the intended benefit for both people; decisions and adaptations that might require practice; competing workplace explanations; access and coverage conditions; unresolved dissent; and evidence needed to distinguish the hypotheses. Keep entries about situations and supports, not named employees.

Example hypothesis: a lead struggles to open a conversation when the concern is ambiguous. A possible learning need is distinguishing observations from interpretations and inviting correction. Rival explanations include unclear expectations, insufficient time to check the concern or fear of contradicting a manager. A next discovery step is to ask whether a fictional example presents a learning difficulty, a workplace barrier or both. No response or result is assumed.

Candidate learning approach
If discovery supports a learning need, consider short, protected practice sessions with participant-chosen fictional scenarios. Candidate supports include an optional example, prompts that can be reduced as desired, another attempt after feedback and a later variation requiring adaptation. These are design hypotheses to review, not a validated prescription. Participants should be able to pause, choose a written format, reject a scenario and challenge feedback. Agree what feedback concerns before practice; do not equate speed, eye contact, confidence or script fidelity with competence.

Evidence boundaries
A later evidence plan should distinguish participant experience, behavior in fictional practice and voluntary accounts of workplace use. Each answers a different question. Self-reported use may inform improvement but cannot alone establish effective transfer or causal benefit. Consider rival explanations such as changed workload, stronger managerial support, selective participation or familiarity with the practice task. Missing evidence must remain unknown, never a deficit. Evidence-sharing choices should be separate from access to learning, with audiences, retention and withdrawal limits established through human review.

Human and system responsibilities
Humans must judge acceptable outcomes, participation conditions, facilitation quality and whether staffing or workflow changes should precede training. Any system should support accessible practice and private reflection while keeping hypotheses, barriers and uncertainty visible. It cannot certify freely chosen participation or determine readiness from activity traces.

Non-AI option and next action
Retain facilitated peer practice with printed fictional scenarios, accessible written alternatives and private reflection. This option also needs covered time and human review. Next, incorporate the distinctions above into the provisional discovery protocol and mapping template, then seek affected-person review before field discovery. Preserve dissent over whether a map is needed at all. Modeling should await an explicit account of which needs remain hypotheses and what evidence is still absent.","prototype_html":"","title":"Understand-stage learning draft: distinguish practice from transfer"},"content_hash":"a18c14b64bc7e98504dcbe6dcc0ed7a8b80810d6642462d7916b013813f91191","id":"understand","parent_revision":null,"revision":1,"trigger_seq":8}}
